name: Superstitious Conditioning
description: Behavior that happens to occur just before a reward is delivered, even when the reward is actually independent of that behavior, can get strengthened and repeated through pure accidental timing -- though a later, larger review finds this classic mechanism is weaker and less well-supported than commonly assumed.
design_relevance_note: Often invoked casually in gamification and habit-app design writing to explain why users attribute a reward to whatever they happened to be doing right before it arrived -- worth flagging as a contested mechanism specifically, not a settled one, before leaning on it as a design justification.
myth_risk_note: A classic, frequently-retold demonstration (Skinner's pigeons) whose specific mechanism a 2022 systematic review found weaker than the popular retelling assumes -- worth flagging precisely because the story is memorable and the underlying mechanism is now in real doubt.
prevalence_note: Referenced occasionally in gamification/behavior-design writing as color/explanation for reward-timing effects, not a load-bearing concept the way variable-ratio reinforcement itself is.

findings.description: A critical review of both laboratory and applied research on response-independent reinforcement schedules found the evidence for Skinner's 'adventitious/accidental reinforcement' mechanism weaker than commonly assumed — the observed behavior patterns are better explained by antecedent stimulus properties and species-typical (e.g. foraging) behaviors than by literal accidental operant reinforcement. Decades of applied practice built on the 'superstition' interpretation may rest on a shakier mechanistic foundation than commonly assumed.
findings.source_title: Bridging the Gap Between Laboratory and Applied Research on Response-Independent Schedules

findings.description: Pigeons given food at fixed time intervals regardless of their own behavior developed distinct, idiosyncratic repeated behaviors (circling, head-thrusting, pecking) — behavior that happened to occur just before food delivery got strengthened and repeated through pure accidental timing, even with no real causal link. Skinner's account for how intermittent, non-contingent reinforcement can produce persistent, seemingly irrational repeated behavior — frequently invoked (accurately or not) to explain compulsive app-checking and notification-driven habits.
